diagrams.title: The GRC Pyramid: From Intent to Execution
diagrams.subtitle: From top to bottom, each level answers a different question. Click a tier to see its exact role.

nodes.label: Guidelines
nodes.detail: Non-binding advice and best practices: they guide policy drafting without creating an obligation. They are cited as a reference, not as a rule.

nodes.label: Policy
nodes.detail: High-level intent approved by leadership and enforceable across the entire organization (AUP, BYOD, IR, privacy...). Its authority comes from executive approval, not its publication.

nodes.label: Standard
nodes.detail: Measurable and verifiable requirement: password length, mandatory encryption, configuration baseline. This is the level that is technically enforced.

nodes.label: Procedure / SOP
nodes.detail: Ordered sequence of repeatable steps for a given task: account revocation, restoration, alert handling. It reduces improvisation under pressure.

nodes.label: Runbook
nodes.detail: Very concrete operational guide, often specific to a system or incident scenario. It is the lowest and most immediately actionable form in the pyramid.

nodes.label: BCP / DRP
nodes.sub: Who does what in a crisis?
nodes.detail: Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plans: roles, timeframes (RTO/RPO), and resources. An untested plan demonstrates no recovery capability.

quiz.question: Which artifact describes the repeatable steps of a task, such as revoking an account?

diagrams.title: Security Policies to Know by Heart
diagrams.subtitle: Eight policies from the §5.1 syllabus. Click a cell to separate the purpose, key rule, and exam trap.

cells.detail: Governs the use of a personal device: connection conditions, separation of work and personal data (container), remote wipe.
Requires device registration, MDM policy enforcement, and explicit user agreement before access.
Always look for the remote wipe and access revocation clause upon employee departure.
Defines what is allowed or prohibited: browsing, email, installed software, data copying.
Must be distributed and accepted, usually during employee onboarding.
It says 'what', not 'how': the technical baseline comes in the standard.

cells.text: No exposed data at the workstation
cells.detail: Requires putting away papers, locking screens, and no visible passwords.
Enforces automatic screen lock and use of secure bins or shredders for paper.
One of the few GRC artifacts with a direct physical effect: link it to a physical control, not a logical one.

cells.text: Roles and responsibilities in a crisis
cells.detail: Defines who triggers, who coordinates, notification timeframes, and escalation channels.
Points to runbooks and the recovery plan; specifies criteria for declaring an incident.
The policy grants authority, the plan gives the course of action: classic multiple-choice distinction.
Classifies data (public, internal, confidential, restricted) and sets retention duration.
Each category has a data owner and an end-of-life rule (return, archiving, destruction).
A backup does not authorize keeping data beyond the legal or contractual duration.
States least privilege, need to know, and the rights approval process.
Requires access reviews and revocation upon role change or departure.
The list of rights lives in the system; the policy sets the general principle.
Defines purging, secure erasure, or physical destruction of drives, USB sticks, and paper documents.
Requires a certificate and an approved vendor, with traceability up to final destruction.
Disposal is among the policies cited in the SY0-801 §5.1 syllabus.
Sets minimal collection, purpose, retention, and data subject rights.
Provides for opt-in/opt-out, access, rectification, erasure, and portability (expanded in §5.4).
Privacy concerns personal data; security covers all assets, including non-personal ones.

diagrams.title: The Risk Register, Thread of the Process
diagrams.subtitle: Five steps that feed a central artifact: the risk register. Follow the loop to see what is recorded at each pass.

nodes.label: Identification
nodes.detail: Lists threats and vulnerabilities that can hit an asset: workshop, inventory, past incident analysis, and threat monitoring.
nodes.exam: An unidentified risk cannot be treated: the most expensive step to miss is the first.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.detail: Estimates impact and likelihood to obtain a risk level, qualitative or quantitative (SLE × ARO = ALE).
nodes.exam: Impact and likelihood are two distinct axes: high likelihood with low impact may remain acceptable.

nodes.label: Treatment
nodes.detail: Selects a response: avoid, reduce (mitigation), transfer (insurance, outsourcing), or accept the risk.
nodes.exam: Acceptance remains valid only if the risk is below the appetite defined by leadership.

nodes.label: Monitoring
nodes.detail: Verifies that chosen controls remain effective and that the environment does not create new risks.
nodes.exam: A control can become obsolete: monitoring detects drift, not just attacks.

nodes.label: Review
nodes.detail: Periodically revisits scores with business owners and approves treatment changes.
nodes.exam: A review is periodic or triggered by a major change, not only after an incident.

nodes.label: Risk Register
nodes.detail: Central artifact recording ID, description, owner, score, chosen treatment, associated controls, and residual risk. Serves as the single source for review and BIA.
nodes.exam: Risk register, SLE/ALE/ARO, and residual risk: SY0-801 §5.2 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

quiz.question: Which artifact centralizes the owner, score, and chosen treatment for each risk?

diagrams.title: Quantitative vs. Qualitative: Two Ways to Quantify Risk
diagrams.subtitle: Two columns, two logics, one final decision. Click each step to see what it brings to the trade-off.

nodes.label: Quantitative
nodes.detail: Numerical approach: assign a monetary value and frequency to the risk to obtain an estimated annual loss.
nodes.exam: SLE, ARO, and ALE: SY0-801 §5.2 syllabus — none of the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Qualitative
nodes.detail: Relative approach: rank the risk on a scale (low, medium, high) based on expert judgment and the risk matrix.
nodes.exam: This is the most common approach when reliable financial data is lacking.

nodes.label: SLE
nodes.detail: Single Loss Expectancy: asset value multiplied by exposure factor (EF). How much does a single incident cost?
nodes.exam: SLE = asset value × exposure factor.

nodes.label: ARO
nodes.detail: Estimated annual frequency of the scenario: number of expected occurrences over one year. An ARO of 0.1 means one incident every ten years.
nodes.exam: ARO is a frequency, not a single-occurrence probability.

nodes.label: ALE
nodes.detail: Annualized Loss Expectancy: SLE × ARO. It gives the maximum rational budget to spend on the control that reduces this risk.
nodes.exam: If a control costs more than the avoided ALE, ROI is negative: classic calculation question.

nodes.label: Scale
nodes.detail: Rating grid shared by stakeholders: it makes risks of very different natures comparable.
nodes.exam: A scale without written definitions of levels produces non-reproducible scores.

nodes.label: Risk Matrix
nodes.detail: Two-way table crossing impact and likelihood to place each risk in a zone (green, yellow, red).
nodes.exam: The red zone generally triggers priority treatment and escalation to leadership.

nodes.label: Experts / Workshop
nodes.detail: Asset owners, CISO, business units, and legal compare judgments to reduce individual bias.
nodes.exam: Qualitative depends on participant quality: involve the asset owner.

nodes.label: Trade-off
nodes.detail: Both approaches converge in the decision: accept, reduce, avoid, or transfer, comparing control cost and residual risk.
nodes.exam: Risk appetite and residual risk: §5.2 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

quiz.question: Which formula gives the Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE)?

diagrams.title: A Third Party's Journey, From Selection to Exit
diagrams.subtitle: A vendor is never 'done' after signing: follow the seven steps and the reassessment loop.

nodes.label: Selection
nodes.detail: Formalizes the need and consults the market: RFI for information, RFP for a proposal, RFQ for pricing, EOI to gauge interest.
nodes.exam: RFP/RFI/RFQ/EOI: SY0-801 §5.3 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Due Diligence
nodes.detail: Assesses security, financial health, certifications, subcontractors, and jurisdiction of the provider before any commitment.
nodes.exam: Due diligence covers the vendor AND its subcontracting chain (fourth party).

nodes.label: Contract
nodes.detail: Sets in writing the scope, service levels, confidentiality, right to audit, incident notification, and exit.
nodes.exam: Without an audit or notification clause, an SLA provides no real means of control.

nodes.label: Access
nodes.detail: Creates the necessary accounts and links for the provider with least privilege, limited duration, and dedicated logging.
nodes.exam: Vendor access must be revoked at the end of the engagement, not just at the end of the contract.

nodes.label: Monitoring
nodes.detail: Track SLAs, review audit reports, verify patches, and reassess third-party risks throughout the relationship.
nodes.exam: Continuous monitoring beats a single annual review: third-party risk evolves between reviews.

nodes.label: Exit
nodes.detail: Revokes access, retrieves and destroys data per the contract, and verifies the return of assets and secrets.
nodes.exam: The exit clause must provide for reversibility before the need even arises.

nodes.label: Third-Party Register
nodes.detail: Single inventory of providers, consumed services, internal owners, contracts, and criticality level.
nodes.exam: Third-party register and vendor lock-in: SY0-801 §5.3 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

quiz.question: Which step verifies controls, financial health, and subcontractors before signing?

diagrams.title: Seven Agreements, Seven Purposes
diagrams.subtitle: SLA, SLO, MOU, MOA, NDA, MSA, SOW: click a cell to distinguish scope, legal force, and the right use case.

cells.detail: Measures the expected service level and provides remedies (service credits) if the target is not met.
This is the agreement where quantified metrics are checked and stipulated penalties are enforced.
On the exam, look first for metrics and remedies, not just the advertised percentage.
Internal or contractual service objective, more flexible than the legal commitment of an SLA.
An SLO alone does not provide penalties: it becomes enforceable when embedded in an SLA.
Set the SLO before negotiating the SLA that will bind the vendor.
Understanding document describing the spirit of a partnership and envisioned responsibilities.
Less formal than a contract, unless expressly stated otherwise in the text.
Used to frame discussion before a formal agreement, not to make financial commitments.
More structured agreement than an MOU, with explicit roles, commitments, and collaboration terms.
Its force depends on the wording: unlike an MOU, it can create obligations.
Typically used between government agencies or institutional partners.
Prohibits disclosure of sensitive information and defines what is considered confidential.
Can be unilateral or mutual (mutual NDA) depending on whether both parties share data.
Sign before sharing architectures, logs, or personal data with a candidate.
Framework contract setting responsibilities, payment, intellectual property, confidentiality, and termination.
Specific agreements (SOWs) attach to it without renegotiating general terms.
MSA/SOW: SY0-801 §5.3 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

cells.text: Deliverables, schedule, price of an engagement
cells.detail: Describes the exact scope of a project: tasks, deliverables, milestones, resources, and acceptance criteria.
The SOW is subordinate to the MSA: in case of conflict, the master agreement often prevails.
A single MSA can carry several distinct SOWs for different engagements.

diagrams.title: Third-Party Limits and Dependencies
diagrams.subtitle: Signing does not eliminate risk: these six factors decide whether you can actually exit and be indemnified.

nodes.label: Jurisdiction
nodes.detail: Country where the vendor and data are based: determines governing law, notification obligations, and cross-border transfers.
nodes.exam: A foreign jurisdiction clause can make an audit right theoretical: check it before signing.

nodes.label: Insurance
nodes.detail: Checks the policy type, caps, exclusions, and proof of coverage (certificate of insurance) of the provider.
nodes.exam: Transferring risk does not erase liability: insurance has caps and exclusions.

nodes.label: ROI
nodes.detail: Compares the cost of the control or migration with the expected benefit and accepted residual risk.
nodes.exam: If the exit cost exceeds the migration benefit, the organization is already in a lock-in situation.

nodes.label: Vendor Lock-in
nodes.detail: Dependency on proprietary formats, APIs, or identities that makes switching vendors long and expensive.
nodes.exam: Vendor lock-in: SY0-801 §5.3 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Reversibility
nodes.detail: Provides for data return in an open format, deletion of copies, and a realistic transition period.
nodes.exam: Demand proof of deletion, not just a contractual promise.

nodes.label: Third-Party Residual Risk
nodes.detail: Even with a good contract, part of the risk remains with the organization: it remains the owner and must bear it.
nodes.exam: Outsourcing a task does not transfer ultimate responsibility to customers or regulators.

quiz.question: Which risk describes the inability to switch vendors without prohibitive cost?

diagrams.title: From Training to Consequence: The Compliance Loop
diagrams.subtitle: A policy without proof of reading or follow-up demonstrates no compliance. Follow the cycle and its remediation loop.

nodes.label: Policy
nodes.detail: The written rule, approved by leadership and distributed: training, legal compliance, privacy, acceptable use.
nodes.exam: An unapproved or undistributed policy is hard to enforce in case of a violation.

nodes.label: Training
nodes.detail: Conveys expected behaviors via LMS, in-person sessions, micro-learning, or targeted campaigns depending on the audience.
nodes.exam: LMS, initial/ongoing/targeted/corrective typologies: §5.6 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Attestation
nodes.detail: Dated signature or acknowledgment proving the person has read and accepted the policy.
nodes.exam: Attestations: SY0-801 §5.4 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Monitoring
nodes.detail: Periodically verifies actual enforcement: audits, access reviews, tests, logs, and training metrics.
nodes.exam: Monitoring detects the gap between the written rule and actual practice.

nodes.label: Consequences
nodes.detail: In case of non-compliance: disciplinary action, privilege revocation, loss of license, legal liability, or regulatory fine.
nodes.exam: Consequences and legal hold: §5.4 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Corrective Training
nodes.detail: Targeted training after a gap or incident, with effectiveness tracking and policy update if needed.
nodes.exam: Corrective training should be proportionate to the observed gap, not automatically company-wide.

quiz.question: Which proof formalizes that the employee has read and accepted the policy?

diagrams.title: Data Subject Rights
diagrams.subtitle: Privacy grants enforceable rights against the organization. Click the central role then each right to see what it implies.

nodes.label: Data Subject
nodes.detail: Any identifiable person whose data is processed. They are the one exercising the rights, not the internal data owner.
nodes.exam: The data subject is the individual; the data owner is the internal party responsible for processing.

nodes.label: Opt-in / Opt-out
nodes.detail: Opt-in: explicit prior agreement before collection. Opt-out: the person refuses after being informed, depending on the legal context.
nodes.exam: Opt-in/opt-out: SY0-801 §5.4 syllabus — none of the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Access
nodes.detail: The person can ask whether their data is being processed, obtain a copy, and know the purposes and recipients.
nodes.exam: Responding within the required timeframe is part of compliance, not just the substance of the response.

nodes.label: Rectification
nodes.detail: Correct inaccurate data or complete incomplete data, then propagate the correction to copies and recipients.
nodes.exam: The correction must be propagated downstream, otherwise the error persists in backups and third-party systems.

nodes.label: Right to Be Forgotten
nodes.detail: Erasure of data when processing is no longer necessary or consent is withdrawn, subject to legal retention obligations.
nodes.exam: Right to be forgotten: §5.4 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books; a legal hold can override it.

nodes.label: Restriction
nodes.detail: Temporarily suspend processing while retaining the data, for example during verification of a dispute.
nodes.exam: Restricting does not erase: the data remains stored but is no longer used.

nodes.label: Portability
nodes.detail: Provide the data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format for transmission to another controller.
nodes.exam: Open format is key: an image PDF is not a machine-readable format.

quiz.question: Which right allows retrieving one's data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format?

diagrams.title: The Flow of a Security Audit
diagrams.subtitle: From scoping to action tracking: six steps that turn evidence collection into verifiable improvement.

nodes.label: Scoping
nodes.detail: Defines the scope, objectives, criteria (framework, policy), stakeholders, and rules of engagement.
nodes.exam: An audit without a written scope drifts: the first question is 'what exactly are we verifying?'.

nodes.label: Collection
nodes.detail: Gathers evidence: logs, configurations, interviews, documents, and scan results, while preserving their integrity.
nodes.exam: Chain of custody and timestamping make the evidence defensible.

nodes.label: Sampling
nodes.detail: Selects a representative subset when the entire population is too large: random, systematic, or risk-targeted.
nodes.exam: A biased sample invalidates the conclusion: always document the selection method.

nodes.label: Testing
nodes.detail: Executes controls: configuration inspection, functional testing, behavioral testing, vulnerability scanning, or interviews.
nodes.exam: A functional test checks what is expected; a behavioral test checks the reaction to an anomaly.

nodes.label: Report
nodes.detail: Presents findings, their criticality, associated evidence, impacts, and prioritized recommendations.
nodes.exam: A finding without evidence and an owner is not actionable.

nodes.label: Follow-up
nodes.detail: Assigns an owner and due date to each action, then verifies remediation during a follow-up audit.
nodes.exam: Follow-up closes the loop: without reassessment, the report remains a snapshot.

quiz.question: Which step selects a representative subset of evidence to test?

diagrams.title: Three Frameworks, Three Questions About Intrusion
diagrams.subtitle: An alert signal feeds three complementary perspectives: phases, techniques, and attribution. Click a column to compare.

nodes.label: Signal / IOC
nodes.detail: Common starting point: an alert, indicator of compromise, or anomalous behavior collected by monitoring.
nodes.exam: An isolated indicator does not tell the whole intrusion story: it must be put into context.

nodes.label: Cyber Kill Chain
nodes.detail: Sequential seven-phase model: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, C2, actions on objectives.
nodes.exam: Key question: 'what phase is the attacker in?'.

nodes.label: Break the Chain
nodes.detail: Each phase offers an opportunity for detection or blocking: the earlier you intervene, the smaller the impact.
nodes.exam: Blocking delivery or exploitation is more effective than waiting for actions on objectives.

nodes.label: MITRE ATT&CK
nodes.detail: Reference matrix of adversary behaviors: the Enterprise matrix has 14 tactics in its current version.
nodes.exam: Key question: 'what technique is the attacker using?'.

nodes.label: Detection Coverage
nodes.detail: Maps rules and sensors onto the matrix to spot blind spots and prioritize new detections.
nodes.exam: The table in the 11 Strategies book shows 11 tactics: that is an older version.

nodes.label: Diamond Model
nodes.detail: Represents the intrusion with four vertices: adversary, victim, capability, and infrastructure, linked by metadata.
nodes.exam: Key question: 'who is attacking what, with what, and from where?'.

nodes.label: Pivot / Attribution
nodes.detail: Allows pivoting from a technical indicator to infrastructure and adversary, then retaining common vertices across incidents.
nodes.exam: Detailed structure not covered by the provided books: remember the four vertices.

quiz.question: Which model links adversary, victim, capability, and infrastructure?

diagrams.title: Pentest Types and Reconnaissance Modes
diagrams.subtitle: Knowledge level first, interaction mode second: everything starts with the rules of engagement.

nodes.label: Rules of Engagement
nodes.detail: Authorization document setting scope, time window, contacts, limits (e.g., no DoS), and escalation procedure.
nodes.exam: Without written authorization, a test becomes unauthorized activity: recurring exam question.

nodes.label: White Box
nodes.detail: The tester knows the architecture, code, and credentials: simulates an insider or an in-depth configuration audit.
nodes.exam: White box = full knowledge; it is the fastest and most targeted scenario.

nodes.label: Gray Box
nodes.detail: Partial knowledge (documents, user access): reproduces an attacker who has already gained an initial foothold.
nodes.exam: Gray box = compromise between realism and efficiency, often the default scenario.

nodes.label: Black Box
nodes.detail: No prior information: the tester acts like an external attacker, from reconnaissance to exploitation.
nodes.exam: Black box = zero knowledge; the longest and closest to a real attack.

nodes.label: Passive
nodes.detail: Reconnaissance without contacting the target: OSINT, public search, DNS records, social media, data leaks.
nodes.exam: Passive = no requests to the target system, so no logs on the victim side.

nodes.label: Active
nodes.detail: Direct interaction: port scanning, fingerprinting, enumeration, vulnerability verification, and controlled exploitation.
nodes.exam: Active = the target sees the activity: hence the importance of the time window and contacts.

quiz.question: Which pentest type gives the tester full knowledge of the system?

diagrams.title: Building a Security Awareness Program
diagrams.subtitle: A program measures first, delivers second, then adjusts. Click each step to see how the loop feeds itself.

nodes.label: Objectives
nodes.detail: Define what you want to change: reporting phishing, locking screens, protecting data, adopting MFA.
nodes.exam: A measurable objective is better than 'general security awareness'.

nodes.label: Baseline
nodes.detail: Starting measurement (quiz, click rate, reporting rate) used as a reference to judge progress.
nodes.exam: Without a baseline, you cannot demonstrate improvement: it is the program's first deliverable.

nodes.label: Channels
nodes.detail: Choose delivery vectors based on the audience: LMS, e-learning, newsletter, posters, workshops, micro-learning.
nodes.exam: LMS and initial/ongoing/targeted typologies: §5.6 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Training
nodes.detail: Tailor content to risk and role: initial, ongoing, role-targeted, or corrective training after an incident.
nodes.exam: Targeted training is more effective than a single module forced on everyone.

nodes.label: Gamification
nodes.detail: Game-like mechanisms (leaderboards, badges, challenges) that boost engagement and retention of behaviors.
nodes.exam: Gamification serves the behavioral objective: it is not an end in itself.

nodes.label: Metrics
nodes.detail: Track participation rate, pass rate, click rate, reporting rate, and time-to-report to measure real effectiveness.
nodes.exam: Reporting rate is a better indicator than click rate alone.

nodes.label: Adjustment
nodes.detail: Revise modules, channels, and targets based on results: an iterative program, not a one-off campaign.
nodes.exam: An effective program is data-driven, not driven by the number of sessions delivered.

quiz.question: Which element measures the starting level before the first training?

diagrams.title: Simulated Phishing Campaign: From Click to Measurement
diagrams.subtitle: A simulation only has value if it leads to immediate learning and actionable metrics.

nodes.label: Target List
nodes.detail: Choose the audience, scenario (BEC, fake portal, quishing), and difficulty based on the baseline and business risk.
nodes.exam: BEC and remote work/OPSEC: SY0-801 §5.6 syllabus — absent from the 4 provided books.

nodes.label: Delivery
nodes.detail: Controlled message delivery with technical tracking: open, click, credential entry, and reporting.
nodes.exam: The simulation must be authorized and scoped like a test, with an escalation contact.

nodes.label: Click
nodes.detail: Measured risky behavior: clicking the link, opening an attachment, or entering credentials on a fake page.
nodes.exam: A click is not a real incident, but it reveals a human vulnerability to address.

nodes.label: Reporting
nodes.detail: The employee uses the report button or notifies the SOC: this is the expected behavior the campaign should reinforce.
nodes.exam: A good program rewards reporting, even when the employee clicked before realizing.

nodes.label: Corrective Training
nodes.detail: Immediate explanation page after a click, or short micro-training after reporting, reminding of good habits.
nodes.exam: Just-in-time remediation is more effective than a module delayed by several weeks.

nodes.label: Metrics
nodes.detail: Calculates click rate, reporting rate, and time-to-report, then compares with the previous campaign and baseline.
nodes.exam: Rising reporting rate and falling click rate = effective program.

quiz.question: Which action turns an accidental click into immediate learning?
